Lessons.Title: More Multiplication
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: assess whether partial-product multiplication of a large whole number is plausible, locate a place-value error in another learner's written work, and then practice products with trailing zeros. The source includes an intentionally unreasonable solution; pupils must critique what they agree and disagree with.
Warm-up: estimate 740×36. Since 740×30=22200, any purported exact product smaller than 20000 is suspect. Estimation is a check, not a replacement for careful multiplication.

Activity 1 — independently authored error critique: a fictional student correctly calculates 740×6=4440 but records the second partial product for the factor 30 as 2220 rather than 22200, then claims the total is6660. Explain why the 3 in 36 represents THREE TENS, so 740×30=22200, and the correct total is26640. Review the student's first partial product without blindly rejecting every step.

Activity 2 — trailing zeros: calculate 670×89 as 67×89×10=59630 and 6700×89 as67×89×100=596300. Explain why increasing one factor tenfold increases the product tenfold and contrast the reasoning with merely guessing a zero count.

Assessment: the learner's diagnostic argument, independently revised working, reasonable estimate and place-value language must be reviewed by a teacher. Numeric products may be checked but do not replace interpreting another student's erroneous written method.

KeyConcepts.Title: Tens digit produces tens partial product
KeyConcepts.Definition: The tens digit 3 in 36 denotes thirty, not three.

KeyConcepts.Title: Factor-of-ten scaling
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplying an integer factor by ten multiplies the product by ten.

KeyConcepts.Title: Estimate before trusting a result
KeyConcepts.Definition: One easy partial product can supply a lower bound for a positive product.

Steps: Correct the tens partial product to 22200 and add.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat a tens-digit partial product as the product with a ones digit
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The digit's position changes factor size by ten.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Judge a result solely because its final digit looks plausible
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Reasonableness depends on magnitude and all partial products.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare the proposed product against 740×30 first.

SummaryPoints: Diagnose the incorrect PLACE VALUE, retaining correct portions of a peer's method.
Check the order of magnitude before computing and correct trailing-zero scaling.
The source's annotated student-work critique requires teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Factors as a Factor in Our Strategy Choice
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: choose a multiplication strategy based on the structure of the particular factors, explain that decision and compare another student's approach. The 2021 source presents products with factors close to 10, 100, round numbers and less convenient combinations so one fixed algorithm is not imposed.
Warm-up: consider 17×9 and17×101. Rather than repeatedly adding, use17×(10−1) and17×(100+1). State the corrections explicitly and explain why the product of 17 by101 must exceed17×100.

Activity 1 — independent set of factor structures: calculate 18×3=54 by a known fact, 18×101=1818 by distribution, 18×25=450 by quarter of18×100, and18×9=162 by compensation from18×10. Compute18×136=2448 by partial products18×(100+30+6). Ask the learner to name a preferred strategy for each and compare its efficiency with standard multiplication.

Activity 2 — contrast products: 29×7=203, 12×45=540, 15×199=2985 and24×154=3696. For15×199 use15×(200−1); for24×154 distribute into 24×(150+4). Highlight why a strategy effective for 15×199 is less attractive for24×154.

Assessment: the official lesson assesses choosing and justifying methods, not merely numeric products. Peer comparisons and claims of efficiency have multiple defensible responses and require teacher evaluation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compensate around friendly factors
KeyConcepts.Definition: A factor just below or above a round ten-power can be replaced by that round number plus a correction.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distributive partial products
KeyConcepts.Definition: A multi-digit factor can be partitioned by place value.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choose a context-appropriate method
KeyConcepts.Definition: The number structure can make a quarter, near-hundred or standard multiplication easiest.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use compensation but omit the correction on every group
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Distributive multiplication requires scaling the correction by the other factor.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Present a numerical answer as a complete strategy comparison
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source asks why an algorithm fits certain factor structures.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Name the chosen property and compare with an alternative.

SummaryPoints: Compare methods on the numbers, not a mandatory one-size-fits-all algorithm.
Use factors near 10/100/200 and known quarters to simplify when justified.
A credible strategy and reasoned comparison need teacher review.

Lessons.Title: More Division
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: revisit partial quotients with multi-digit divisors, judge whether another learner's division answer can be reasonable, and explain which large partial products have been subtracted. A student-written long-division layout may contain a correct remainder calculation but a wrong place value in the hundreds portion.
Warm-up: use 13×500=6500 to estimate 6773÷13. Any positive quotient much smaller than500 cannot be correct because more than6500 was available to partition.

Activity 1 — diagnostic learner critique: an original false partial-quotient calculation for 6773÷13 subtracts 6500 correctly but labels its partial quotient as50 instead of500; it then subtracts260 (20 groups), leaving13, and subtracts13 (1 group). Recording50+20+1=71 is wrong, while500+20+1=521 is correct. Explain the value of each subtracted chunk, not just its written position.

Activity 2 — independent division: divide 7392 by24 using partial quotients. Subtract24×300=7200, leaving192; subtract24×8=192, leaving zero. Conclude308. Alternatively use24×(300+8)=7392; compare partial-quotient methods with a peer.

Assessment: numerical quotient and inverse check can be verified, but the selected partial-quotient chunks, estimation of order of magnitude and critique of a fictional student solution require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Partial quotient records number of groups
KeyConcepts.Definition: Subtract divisor×a chosen group count; the written partial quotient must represent the correct magnitude.

KeyConcepts.Title: Combine valid partial quotients
KeyConcepts.Definition: When the remainder reaches zero, add all partial group counts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Verify by multiplication
KeyConcepts.Definition: Divisor multiplied by quotient should reproduce the dividend for exact division.

WorkedExamples.Title: Detect wrong magnitude
WorkedExamples.Question: A learner records71 for6773÷13 while subtracting chunks6500,260 and13. Correct the reasoning.

WorkedExamples.Method: Original Grade 5 explanation. Exact computation is only a supporting check; critique, diagrams and independent strategy decisions are teacher-reviewed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Write 50 as the quotient associated with subtracting 6500 by13
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label the chosen group count500 explicitly.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Accept a small division quotient when the dividend is thousands and divisor about ten
CommonMistakes.Correction: Estimate with known divisor multiples before or after dividing.

SummaryPoints: Partial quotients can be chosen in different valid sizes but must sum to the true quotient.
A place-value critique is distinct from checking only the remainder.
Peer explanations and annotated chunking are teacher-reviewed.
